# Space Atrapos - Pilot's guide

# basics | Getting started
Your first steps, the controls, and how this guide and the game's tooltips work.

## start | Welcome, pilot | keywords: New game, Continue, Load, Settings, Exit to desktop
You are an automaton built by Ephestos in **New Hellas** - a galaxy of 120 star systems where six Greek star empires, the independents and the pirates compete. There's no story to follow: the galaxy is yours to make your way in. A new game starts you **on foot on Amnissos**, the green ocean world of the Minoans' home system, Knossos, by a city's landing field - with no ship yet, your pulse rifle, your mining beam and your scanner. Earn your first ship by mining and couriering (see [Making a living](doc:sandbox)); the **tutorial** walks you through it, step by step (see [The tutorial](doc:tutorial)). Everything is in 3D, seen over your shoulder on foot or from behind your ship.

- **The title screen**: **New game**, **Continue** (your latest save), **Load**, **Settings**, the **Archive** (this guide and the other books), **Talos** (the game's editor) and **Exit**.
- **The Esc menu** (in a game): resume, save, load, settings, back to the title screen, **Exit to desktop**.
- **Saving**: **Esc > Save** into one of the slots; the game also **autosaves** when you dock and when you come through a gate. A save keeps the galaxy (its economy, the war, your reputation), your ship, cargo and drachmas, your missions and where you are.
- **Settings**: the window and **Anti-aliasing** (off, FXAA, MSAA 2x/4x/8x, TAA - MSAA 2x at first: smooth edges, a steady starfield), text sizes, the volumes, the controls, the FPS counter.
- **The interface** is the same everywhere: your **health gauge** top left (hull, shields and fuel in space - the automaton's health on foot - and beside it the ship's readout), the **compass bar** top centre (in the ship and on foot), the ship's **sights** in the middle, the **event log** bottom left, the **toolbar** at the bottom (the ship's in it, the automaton's on foot - see [the toolbars](doc:computer)), messages in the middle. Bottom right, icons (each with its key over it) open the Automaton's **inventory** (Tab), the **planet map** and the **solar map** (M), the **galaxy map** (G) and the [tutorial](doc:archive) (with the mouse free - a right click - to click them). There is no help text on screen; this guide is **F1**.
- Lose your ship and you're back by the system's first station, in a whole ship.
- **Talos**, the game's editor, opens from the title screen, from the **Esc menu** in a game, or with **F8**.

![](shot:space3d)

## guide-tooltips | Tooltips and this guide
Buttons show icons: hover one for half a second to see its tooltip - its name, its keyboard shortcut in brackets and what it does.
- **Keep hovering for 12 seconds** and the tooltip **pins**: it stays when you move away and its links can be clicked. Close it with its blinking ✕, a right-click or a click outside it - or just open another tooltip.
- The links open this guide at the right page. **Back / Forward** (the arrows, Alt+Left / Alt+Right, or the mouse's side buttons) move through the pages you've read, like a web browser.
- **F1** opens the guide at the page for where you are (space, a station, the Automaton, a planet).

## archive | The Archive: every book in one place | keywords: Archive, Search every book, Pilot's Guide, Tutorial, Encyclopedia, Controls, Versions, Talos Manual
This guide is one of the books of the **Archive** - all of the game's documentation in one window. Its shelf: the **Pilot's Guide** (how everything works), the **Tutorial** (first steps, lesson by lesson), the **Encyclopedia** (ships, stations, gear, worlds and the lore of ancient Greece - only what you've discovered, each with its picture), **Controls** (every action and the keys and buttons bound to it now), **Versions** (what each version of the game brought, patch by patch) and the **Talos Manual** (the game's editor). **Search every book** finds the pages, in all of them, that have all your words. Links lead to any book's pages; **Back / Forward** retrace your steps. Open it with **F1** (at the page for where you are), a **Guide** button, the **Archive** tab of the Automaton or the Field Computer, or **Archive** in the Esc menu and on the title screen.


## controls | Controls
- **Flying:** the mouse is a **virtual stick** - move it off the middle and the ship pitches and turns, faster the further out (**C** or the middle button centres it). **A / D** roll. **W / S** set the throttle (it stays where you leave it, and stops at **zero** on the way through: let go and press **S** again for reverse thrust - a negative throttle; **X** stops), **Shift** boosts. **R / F** (or **Space / Ctrl**) fire the thrusters up and down, **Q / E** sideways. **J** the [Hyperion drive](doc:space). **T** targets what's nearest the middle of the view. The **left button** fires; **1-9** use the [toolbar's](doc:computer) slots.
- **Landing and docking:** **L** lands (low and slow over level ground) and takes off; near a station it asks for a [landing pad](doc:stations) instead (again: cancels).
- **Aboard and on foot:** **U** stands up from the pilot's seat (landed, docked or in flight - the ship flies on). **W A S D** walk where the camera looks, **Q / E** strafe, **Shift** runs, **Space** jumps - hold it and your **jet pack** fires, the mouse looks round. The **left button** is context-sensitive: when something is in reach - a terminal, a person, the pilot's seat, a package, a cave's mouth, a chest - the sights turn into a **grabbing hand** and a click uses it; otherwise it fires your rifle (or the beam). **Z** pulses your **scanner** (or the scanner in hand - **4** - and the left button). The [builder](doc:building) in hand (**5**): **N** its pieces, **K** turns the piece, **O** build / demolish / upgrade / paint, **P** snapping. **Y** locks or unlocks a door or gate you built.
- **Camera:** the **wheel** moves it in and out; in your ship hold the **right button** to look round.
- **The free mouse:** a **right click** frees the mouse - the cursor shows, and it's yours to use: **click** something (a station, a planet, a ship, a gate) to make it your target; **hold the left button and drag** to steer the ship or turn your view as the captured mouse does. A **right click** again captures it. (Holding the right button and dragging still turns the camera - only a click frees or captures.) Leaving the window (Alt+Tab) lets the mouse go too; click back in to capture it.
- **Windows:** **Tab** or **I** the [Automaton](doc:computer) · **Esc** closes the open window, else the menu · **F1** this guide.
- **In menus:** **W/A/S/D** or the arrows move between buttons, **Enter** or **Space** presses it, **Q / E** switch tabs.
- **Gamepad:** the left stick steers (and walks), the triggers set the throttle, **A** boosts, **Y** the Hyperion drive, **B** stops.
- **Rebinding:** keys, mouse buttons (the free mouse's too) and gamepad buttons can be changed in **Settings > Controls**.

# space-ch | In space
The 3D star systems: flying, the Hyperion drive, fighting, the monsters of the void.

## spaces | The 3D game: systems, planets, stations | keywords: Hyperion drive, gravity well, virtual stick
A star system is built around you in 3D, at its true size - its star, planets and moons, stations, gates and asteroid fields, the traffic between them - and you fly all of it from behind your ship:
- **Planets are real ground** - every planet and moon is a whole world of procedural terrain: continents and seas, mountain ranges, craters, ice caps, lava. What you see from orbit is the ground you fly down to: it grows finer as you come closer, down to a metre underfoot - no loading, no break. Gas giants have no ground, only cloud bands.
- **Stations** are kilometres across, with landing pads and hangars (see [Docking](doc:stations)).
- **Gates** - fly through a gate's ring to jump to the system it leads to (the [galaxy map](doc:galaxy) plots routes).
- **Markers** show the star, planets, stations, gates, ships, the towns of the planet you're near and the [unknown bio-signatures](doc:signals); **T** targets what's nearest the middle of the view - its distance and time to arrive in its window.
- **Your ship is walkable** - a Minoan armoured hauler, ~58 m long. Stand up from the captain's throne (**G**) and walk it: the **bridge** in the nose (the throne on its lit dais, crew seats at the consoles under the windows, the bull's banners, the star map's hologram), the **quarters** through the arch (bed, couch, shelves), the **loading bay** (your cargo in crates under the crane) and the tail's door. Its **terminals** open the Automaton's pages and the ship's devices - the **Fabricator** and the **Star Map** on the bridge, **Inventory** and **Refinery** in the bay. The door at the back slides up and the ramp lowers to the ground: walk down it to get out, up it to board.
- **Your target's window** - lock on (**T**) and a window opens top left under the gauge: the target live, a camera circling it, and its card - a ship's or a creature's shields, hull, speed, weapons; a planet's or a star's type, size, orbit; a station's trade and free pads.

![](shot:space3d_ground)

## space | Flying and fighting | keywords: Hyperion drive, Land on, land
- **Steering** - the mouse is a virtual stick (the sights' inner ring): off the middle, the ship pitches and turns. **A / D** roll, **W / S** the throttle, **Shift** boosts, **X** stops. Flight assist keeps your course along your nose.
- **The compass bar** (top centre): your **heading**, the compass points scrolling past the notch and the degrees in the box under it - flying, where your nose points; on foot, where you look. Near a world north is its north pole; out in space it's the system's north, on its plane. Inside a ship, a station or below ground it's hidden.
- **The sights** (the middle): the crosshair and the rings round it, the stick's mark inside the inner ring, the distance to your target (or to the ground your nose points at) under the middle. Left, **VEL** - your speed on its curved bar (full at the Hyperion drive's top); right, **ALT** - your height over the nearest world (named under it), or how far it is when you're out in space.
- **The readout** beside your health gauge: the drive (flight, boost, Hyperion charging, the gravity well holding it back), the throttle; near a planet your **latitude and longitude**; the **heat**, your **weapons and their ammo** (your target: in its own window under it).
- **The Hyperion drive** - **J**: after a two-second charge the ship races across the system at up to 250 km/s - any planet in seconds. Target something first (**T**) and the drive takes you there: it turns the nose to it while you leave the mouse alone (it engages once you're lined up), steers round anything in the way, slows by itself as you arrive and drops you out about 1.5 km from it. **Gravity** holds it back: every planet, moon and the star has a **gravity well** (a dozen times its radius) - the deeper in, the slower (the readout names the well). Coming too close to anything, or being shot, drops you out.
- **The star's heat** - fly close to the star (within two and a half of its radii) and your ship heats up (the readout's heat bar): hot, it burns your shields, then your hull.
- **Weapons** are your ship's real fittings - the weapons on its hardpoints (Outfitting), each with its own damage, rate and colour; missiles use ammo. The **left button** fires; a weapon on the toolbar - its key (**1-9**) or a click - switches that kind on and off. With a ship targeted, a ring shows where to aim to hit it.
- **Shields** soak hits and come back a few seconds after the last; the **hull** doesn't. Your ship's class, modules and tech set its hull, shields and speed.
- **Traffic** - traders ply between the stations and set down on their pads, the system's **patrols** circle them, and now and then **pirate raiders** come for you (more in lawless systems). A raider destroyed pays its **bounty**.
- **Landing** - low (within 160 m) and slow (under 80 m/s) over dry, level enough ground clear of trees and boulders, **L** sets the ship down on its legs. See [On the surface](doc:planets).

![](shot:space3d_fight)

## damage | Health, shields and fuel | keywords: Accuracy, Critical, Miss
**Your health gauge** (top left) - your ship's outline, filled with red as high as its **hull** is, inside a ring of blue as high as its **shields** are, and round that a ring of amber as high as your **fuel** is - hover the rings for the numbers. On foot the same gauge shows the automaton's health. Beside it, the ship's [readout](doc:space).

## signals | Unknown bio-signatures: the old monsters | keywords: Unknown bio-signature
Every system has its **unknown bio-signatures** - markers on your screen ("Unknown bio-signature", and how dangerous: easy, moderate, hard, insane). **T** targets one; the Hyperion drive takes you there. Each is the lair of one of the old monsters, hundreds of metres long, swimming the void: the **Void Leviathan** (a plated whale-serpent with glowing veins and tentacles round its maw), **Cetus** (the armoured sea monster Poseidon sent against Andromeda), **Charybdis** (a ring of teeth round a turning vortex), **Skylla** (a sea witch crowned in gold on eight great tentacles), **the Hydra** (eight serpent heads on a knot of coils), **Cerberus** (the three-headed hound in gold), **the Chimera** (lion, goat and serpent in one), **Echidna** (the mother of monsters, half woman, half serpent) and **the Minotaur** (the bull-headed giant crowned in bronze).

- Come within a few kilometres and it comes for you. It keeps its distance, circling; its glow gathers - then it looses **orbs**: a **ring** round you with a gap in the middle (hold still, or slip through), a **fan**, a **spiral**, a **bloom** in every direction. The orbs are slower than your ship, and only their heart can hit you - hard to dodge, always dodgeable. Come too close and it rams you.
- Its **shields** come back if you let up; its **hull** doesn't. Hit it anywhere along its body. Slain, it pays its bounty (bigger for the harder ones) and its signature is gone.

![](shot:space3d_monster)

## mining | Mining asteroids | keywords: Mining, asteroid, vein, Scanned, resonance, Fragments, Rubble
Most systems have **asteroid fields** - iron, titanium or platinum rocks, a few hundred to a field. Fire with your sights on a rock within 1.5 km and your ship cuts it with its red **mining beam** instead of its guns; the rock becomes your target (**T** on one does too).

- **The scan** - stay within 3 km of your targeted rock for two seconds and it's scanned: what it's made of, and its **veins**, marked on the rock as it tumbles. An unscanned rock gives only **rubble**.
- **Cutting a vein** - the beam cuts the vein nearest your sights. Over the toolbar the readout shows its **heat** on a bar with the cutting band in **green**: below it the vein cuts slowly; in it at full speed, and **resonance** builds the longer you hold it there; above it the beam strains - and at the top the vein **fractures**, a share of it lost as rubble. Let go to let it cool: fire in pulses to keep it in the green. Harder minerals heat faster.
- **Fragments** go into your hold, until it's full. Sold as they are they fetch little: an on-board **refinery** ([the ship's devices](doc:industry)) makes minerals of them.
- The rock is **carved** as you mine it: each vein you cut sinks into a **pit**, deeper and wider the more of it comes out (its mark sits at the bottom), fractures blow chunks out of it, and hacking at the bulk rock leaves craters where the beam strikes. Mined out, it's **gone** for good - your pits and craters are kept in your save.

![](shot:space3d_mining)

## digging | Mining on foot | keywords: deposit, crystal, ore, mining beam, overheated, Dug
On a planet's ground stand **deposits** of its minerals - **crystal clusters** (ice, salt, sulphur, obsidian, orichalcum) and **boulders veined with ore** (iron, copper, tin, silver, gold, cobalt, titanium, platinum). Which ones depends on the kind of world: ice and salt on frozen ones, sulphur and obsidian on volcanic ones, metals on cratered worlds and moons. They're always in the same places, so you can come back to them.

- **Fire** with your sights on a deposit within 30 m: your **mining beam** cuts it instead of the rifle. Its ore goes straight into your pack as the **mineral itself** - nothing to refine.
- The deposit **shrinks** as you cut it, and at the last unit it breaks up and is **gone** for good.
- Beside the sights: the deposit and what's **left** of it, the beam's **heat** and what you've **dug**. The beam heats as it cuts (harder minerals faster); at the top it **overheats** and stops until it has cooled right down - let go now and then.

![](shot:space3d_dig)

## terrain | Digging the ground | keywords: Terrain digger, dig, tunnel, cave, voxel, vein, ghost
**V** swaps your rifle for the **terrain digger** (again: the rifle). Fire and its beam **carves the ground** where your sights are - a sphere out of it at a time. Hold it on one spot and it bores in along the beam: **down** into a pit, or **into a hillside** as a tunnel. Sweep it and it cuts a **trench**. Where you've dug, the ground is solid **voxels**, so you can make pits, tunnels, caves and overhangs, and walk in them: you stand on their floors, their walls stop you, and the camera stays inside. Plants and boulders in the way go. You can't dig in a town. It shares the mining beam's **heat**, so let go before it overheats. Everything you dig stays dug - it's kept in your save.

**Veins.** Under the ground lie **veins** of the world's minerals - a few metres down, a ragged lode with tendrils of ore branching out of it every way, far richer than a deposit on the surface (40 units and more). The **scanner** shows the veins near you as a **hologram** through the ground for a minute - each one's shape in 3D, a wireframe over a glassy body in its mineral's colour, dimmer the more of it you've dug - marked with its name, what's in it and how deep: dig down to it with the terrain digger, and every carve that cuts into it puts its ore in your pack. Dug into, a vein shows as **solid ore** in the walls and floor of your pit. What's left of each vein is kept in your save.

![](shot:space3d_digging)

![](shot:space3d_vein)

## building | Building | keywords: Builder, build, foundation, wall, ceiling, roof, stairs, pillar, demolish, upgrade, paint, snapping, tier, timber, stone, marble, bronze, chest, bed, workbench, kiln, brazier
The **builder** (**5** on the toolbar) puts up buildings of your own anywhere on a world's open ground (not in a town), out of modular **pieces** that snap together on a **4 m grid** - each storey **3.2 m**. In hand, a **preview** of the piece shows where it would go, snapped to the nearest place it fits on what's built: **green** when it can go there, **red** when it can't - the panel at the bottom says why (nothing holds it up, too far from a support, its place taken, the ground too high, what it costs that you don't have). A **click** places it; **hold the button and drag** to lay a whole run - a wall's length along its edge, a rectangle of foundations or floors - placed when you let go.

**The pieces** (**N**: the builder's menu, by category, each with its picture and cost): **foundations** - square, **half** (4 x 2 m), **quarter** (2 x 2 m) and **triangle** (a triangle's slanted edges take more pieces at 30 degrees: angled and rounded layouts) and **front steps**; **floors and ceilings** (square, half, quarter, triangle, a **hatch** with a ladder down) - halves and quarters for balconies and odd gaps, snapping along an edge in half and quarter steps; **walls** - full, half (a parapet), an **upper wall** hanging from a ceiling, a sloped **gable wall** under a roof; **doors and windows** - a doorway, a **door**, a **window** with shutters, an **archway**, a great **gate**; **roofs** - sloped, **hip** and **valley** corners, a **pyramid** cap, a triangle's, flat; **stairs** - straight, **spiral**, a **ramp**, a **ladder**; **supports** - **pillars** (your style's columns) and **beams** between them; **fences** - a balustrade, a fence, a fence gate; and **furniture**: a **brazier** and a **wall lamp** (they light the rooms), a **chest** (it keeps things: a click opens it), a **bed** (rest - health and stamina back - and you wake there when you're downed on that world), a **workbench** and a **kiln** (your ship's **fabricator** and **refinery**, at home), a table, a bench, a storage jar.

**Snapping:** foundations snap beside foundations and stand level, reaching down into the ground on a slope; walls go on a foundation's or a floor's edges - or on the wall under them; ceilings on the walls' tops (or beside another ceiling); pillars on corners; stairs in a square cell. **K** (or the middle button) turns the piece - a quarter for squares and stairs, a half for walls and doors (a door's swing, a gable's slope), 30 degrees for furniture. **P** turns snapping off: furniture and foundations go just where you aim.

**Support:** foundations stand on the ground; walls, pillars and beams carry what's over them; a ceiling or roof rests on walls, pillars or beams - and reaches out from them a cell at a time, weaker each cell: **timber** reaches 1 cell past a support, **stone** and **marble** 2, **bronze** 3. A piece nothing holds up can't be placed. Take a piece down and whatever only it held up **comes down with it** (the preview warns you how many).

**Tiers and styles:** every piece in four **tiers** - **timber** (half-timbered, plastered: timber from the trees the terrain digger fells), **stone** (your style's walls, frieze and cornice: building stone - every carve of the terrain digger cuts a block loose), **marble** (stone and marble blocks) and **bronze** (stone and bronze ingots - the fabricator casts them) - each tougher and reaching further than the last; and in any empire's **style**: Minoan, Athenian, Spartan, Mycenaean, Ionian, Cycladic (its colours, columns, frieze, roof tiles). A **paint** colours the plaster, wood and tiles.

**O** switches the builder's **mode**: **build**; **demolish** (the piece under the sights lit amber - a click takes it down: half its cost back, all of it within a minute of placing it); **upgrade** (to the next tier, for the difference); **paint** (with the paint chosen in the menu). Doors, gates, shutters and hatches open and shut with a click (the builder put away). What you build is kept in your save and stands there when you come back.

**Locks:** **Y** by a door, gate, fence gate or hatch you built locks it (shutting it first) - and again unlocks it. Locked, it won't open (its prompt shows a padlock) - for you until you unlock it, and never for anyone else: the predators and raiders that come after you push an unlocked door open and walk in.

**Wear:** bolts - yours and your enemies' - and the terrain digger's beam wear down what they hit, by each piece's toughness (its tier: timber the weakest, bronze the toughest). Past each quarter of its toughness a piece shows it: soot, then cracks across it. At nothing left it **breaks** - and whatever only it held up comes down with it. There's no mending: **upgrading** a piece to its next tier makes it whole again (the demolish and upgrade panel shows how sound it is).

![](shot:space3d_building)

# stations-ch | Stations
Everything you can do while docked.

## stations | Docking | keywords: Undock
Stations are big - two kilometres and more across - and each empire builds its own: the **Minoans** a great ring with the wave frieze round a tower of stacked discs; **Athens** a marble ring under navy roofs with four temples on it and a round colonnade in the middle, the owl on its crown; **Sparta** an eight-sided fortress of iron under cream and crimson armour, a bastion at each corner, gold spear tips, the lambda on its keep; **Mycenae** a citadel of great stone blocks round a beehive dome, gold rosette shields on its arms; **Ionia** an armillary - a slim marble ring, a lapis dome with gold rings turned round it, arms ending in volutes; the **Cyclades** a spiral of white marble winding out from a dome with a marble figure on it; the **Sea Peoples** a broken ring of dark iron, bone spikes, the skull. Four platforms of numbered **landing pads** stand out from the ring - two of them big enough for the largest freighters - floodlit. Their parts are solid: fly into one and you bounce off it, hurt. The empires' **ships** differ as much: Athens' scythe wings and temple-carrying traders, Sparta's lambda shields and gun barrels, the Minoan double-axe blades, Mycenae's boar tusks and gold domes, Ionia's column across the hull, the Cyclades' smooth marble with oars of ribs, the raiders' spikes and tattered sails.
- **Ask for a pad** - near a station, **L**: traffic control gives you one (the smallest free one that takes your ship); it lights up and is marked on your screen (an arrow at the edge when it's off it). **L** again cancels.
- **Set down on it yourself** - fly over it and come down on the thrusters: **R / F** up and down, **Q / E** sideways. Within 600 m of it the **landing display** shows: the pad **from above** with your ship in the middle, nose up (steer the square under you; a line shows your drift), the **height tape** with how fast you climb or sink, the **level bubble** (keep it in its ring) and your **speed**, the thrust (signed: backward and down negative), your **heading** - how far your nose is off the pad's axis - and what still stops a touchdown. Every ship sets down **square on its pad**: the nose to the pad's **top** (toward the station - the bold edge, the chevron painted on the deck), the engines to its bottom, never across it; the display shows the pad's axis and chevron, and HEADING turns green within **12°**. In the view the pad is outlined, and a line drops from your ship to the deck under it. Inside its square, lined up with it, level with it and slower than **12 m/s**, you touch down - and the pad's **lift** takes your ship down into the station's **hangar**.
- **The port** - the pad's **lift** carries your ship down its shaft into the **port** hung under the platform, the shutters sliding shut over you: no cut, you ride all the way down. Get up from your seat (**G**) and walk down the ramp into its **hall**, in the empire's own look - pillars or columns, its frieze and banners, its emblem great on the wall, stacks of crates, a gantry crane - where the lifts bring the ships down: yours, and the traders' parked beside it. The **Workshop** terminal stands by the middle door. Through the doors: the **concourse** (windows back onto the ships) and a row of rooms with windows out to space - the **services hall** (the **Market**, **Outfitting**, the **Shipyard**, the **Designer**, **Reputation** at their terminals - click one), the **bar**, the **lounge**, the **harbour office** (**Missions**) and the **stores**. Docking recharges your shields.
- **Its people** - nobody appears from nowhere: everyone in the port **works there** (the bartender, harbour officers, guards at the doors, dock workers, cargo hands - on shift), **lives there** (their families, in the bar and the lounge), or **came in on a ship** down on one of the platform's lifts - its captain and crew walk out of it when it lands, go about the port, work the terminals, and go back aboard before it lifts off. Each is one of the sector's people, with a name, an age, a family, friends, savings and a life that goes on when you're not looking: they take jobs, sign on to ships, buy ships of their own, marry, have children, enlist at war, grow old. Click one to **talk**: who they are (their work, their family, their friends, what happened to them lately), the **news** of the sector, and **work** - one of the station's missions, its pay; accept it there and then.
- **Undock** - back aboard, **L** or **Space**: the shutters open over you, up the lift onto your pad, and off.
- **The law** - every station is armed: heavy turrets at its platforms' corners. Fire on a trader or a patrol near a station and you're **fined** (250 dr; what you can't pay you owe - no pad till it's paid). **Destroy** one, or fire on a station you're not at war with, and you're **wanted** in that system for a quarter of an hour: its stations open fire on you - they will destroy you - its patrols hunt you, no station will take you. Stations of an empire that counts you an enemy fire on you too.
- **War** - an enemy's invasion fleet besieging a system is there in ships: its **warships** circle the station they besiege, firing on it, its guns answering; a station worn down **burns**. Come near one in trouble and it **hails** you: its **defence** and **repair** jobs, well paid - destroy its besiegers, bring the goods its crews need.
- Traders use the pads too: you'll see them come in, set down, sit a while and lift off - the haulers, the biggest of them, on the big pads. They're the economy's own ships, each with its captain and crew: lock on to one (**T**) and its card shows its name, captain and crew, and where it's bound. Follow its people back aboard, then the ship to its next port - through the gates, system to system - and its crew walks out there.
- **Aboard a trader** - down in the port, a trader stands on its legs with its stern ramp lowered while it's in port: walk up it and you're aboard. Its rooms are fitted inside its own hull, as wide and as high as the hull leaves room for: a corridor from the door, the **cargo hold** (its crates along the sides), the **crew quarters** (bunks), the **bridge** at the nose (the pilot's seat, its consoles). The map shows where it is and where it's bound. **Stay aboard and it takes you with it** - up its lift, across the system, through the gates to other systems - and when it goes down into its next port, walk down its ramp into that port. You can't save aboard a moving ship. Beside the pilot's chair is a **passenger seat**: sit in it (click it) and you watch the ship from outside - move the mouse to look round it, the wheel to come closer or go further; any move key gets you up.
- **Your ship stays where you left it** - docked at the station you rode away from, even in another system; the map shows where it is. **B** there recalls it: it comes to you (from another system, a while longer - a jump takes time), waits for a free pad of your port and comes down its lift.

## workshop | Workshop | keywords: Workshop, Upgrade, Refuel, Pump
The **WORKSHOP** (its terminal on the port's deck) has two pages:

- **UPGRADES** - every part of your ship and your automaton carries **stats** you can raise, five levels each, dearer each level: some fifty of them - hull and shields, armour and every resistance, shield recharge and its delay, speed, handling, **evasion**, weapon damage, rate of fire, range, **accuracy**, **critical chance** and **critical damage**, system cooldowns, fuel tank and fuel efficiency, hold space, probe strength, ore yield, mining and refinery speed; the automaton's health, healing, damage, rate of fire, reach, accuracy, walking speed, evasion, armour and resistances. Pick the ship or the automaton, then a part. **Upgrade Kits** made on board fit them too (see [Industry](doc:industry)).

- **FUEL**: **Refuel** fills your tank at this station's fuel price (a tenth of its market price for a unit of fuel, per unit of tank); **Pump fuel from the hold** empties the fuel you carry into the tank (10 a unit).

## market | Market | keywords: Buy 1, Buy 10, Sell 1, Sell all, Trade routes
Every station has a live **commodities market**. New Hellas trades in **140 goods** in ten categories of fourteen - **Food & drink** (grain, olive oil, wine, honey, garum, saffron...), **Medicine** (dittany of Crete, nanomeds, Asklepian salve...), **Machinery**, **Technology** (processors, star reckoners, automaton brains...), **Energy** (deuterium, Greek fire, antimatter pods...), **Minerals** (copper, tin, silver, orichalcum, Parian marble...), **Luxuries** (silk, Tyrian purple, amber, red-figure vases, lyres...), **Arms**, **Wares & salvage** and **Exotics** (hydra scales, cyclops lenses, ambrosia...). A station deals in the original goods and in what its economy **produces** (cheap here, marked MADE HERE) and **uses** (dear here) - a research station in different goods from a mining colony, so hauling between them pays; a station also buys whatever you bring it. A **tab per category** (with how many of its goods this station trades) shows that category's goods - **Sell** (what the station pays you), **Buy** (what it asks; "-" when it has none), the **galactic average** price with how far this station's price is from it (green ▲: it pays more than average - a good place to sell; red ▼: less), **Supply** (bars and the station's stock) and **Demand** (bars: how badly the station needs it - only goods it uses), and what you carry. Click a good (or **W/S**, the arrows, the D-pad) to see it on the right: its prices, a quantity (**A/D**, or − / + / MAX; Shift + A or Shift + the arrows: by 10), **Buy** (Enter / pad A) and **Sell** (Backspace / pad X), and the **best prices within two jumps** - with the profit a unit over today's price here, and a button to plot a route there. Prices follow supply, and your own trades move them too: every unit you buy pushes the price up, every unit you sell pushes it down (harder where the good is scarce), and the push fades over a few minutes - so a full hold usually pays best sold across several stations. System states (boom, famine, war...) move prices. Most of what a station uses is shipped in by the NPC traders (and you); a station short of its inputs slows down and uses less.

- **Trade routes** (only what you know: a run starts at a station whose market you know - you've docked there - and ends at one you've found, come within sensor range of; be **Friendly** with an empire and it shares all of its markets): the sector map (M) and the galaxy map (G) have a trade layer (the cart button, or **T**): green arrows for the best runs - buy a good at one station, sell it at another - labelled with the good and the profit a unit. See their pages.

## outfitting | Outfitting | keywords: Fit, Remove, Buy Missiles
- **Tabs**: Your ship (fitted modules and ship gear in your hold) · Weapons · Systems · Ship modules · Automaton gear · Supplies. Click a card to see it on the right: a large picture of it, its price and buttons, what it is, a weapon's or system's own stats, and **before → after** - every stat it would change (green better, red worse), worked out with your ship's (or automaton's) real numbers.

- **Weapons come in sizes** - **XS, S, M, L, XL, XXL** - and go on the ship's **hardpoints**, each of a size too: two XS on an interceptor, three on the Atrapos (one S, two XS), four on a gunship (two M, two S), ten on a frigate, 14 on a cruiser, 18 on a battleship and **24 on a dreadnought** (two XXL). A weapon fits a hardpoint **its size or bigger**. Each size up hits 1.7 times harder, reaches a little further and fires a little slower - and costs 2.6 times as much. Not every kind comes in every size: Pulse Cannons XS-XL, Plasma Cannons and Missiles XS-XXL, the Beam Emitter S-XXL, the Electro and the Bouncer Plasma S-XL. A weapon is an item like any other: bought at an outfitter (the **WEAPONS** tab, a size at a time - it goes on a free hardpoint that takes it, else into your hold), salvaged from wrecks, sold; in the hold, click it (or drag it onto a free hardpoint on the equipment screen) to fit it; right-click a fitted one to take it out.


- Every fitting has its **area** of the ship: **weapons** on its **hardpoints** (the wings), weapon modifiers and sensors in the **nose**, armour and shields in the **hull**, the drive's modules (Enhanced Thrusters, Afterburner, Star Energizer) at the **thrusters**, cargo racks, fuel tanks and the Salvage Rig in the **cargo bay**. How many each area takes depends on the hull class. The Automaton's inventory shows them as an **equipment screen**: your ship drawn large with each area's slots beside it - drag ship gear from the hold onto a free slot of its area.
- **Modules** come in ratings **E** (cheap) to **A** (best): shield generators, hull reinforcement, cargo racks, thrusters, shield cell banks...
- **Remove** sells a fitted item back for 80% of its price; **hold** takes a fitted module out into your hold instead (it's gear - see Gear). **Supplies** (missiles, energy drinks) don't use cargo space.

## gear | Gear: equipment for your ship and your automaton | keywords: Quality, Loadout, Ship gear, Weapon mod, Armour, Core, Passive, resistance


**Gear** is equipment you fit to your **ship** or equip on your **automaton** (you on foot). Every piece comes in a **quality** from **E** (common) through D, C and B to **A** (masterwork): the better, the stronger - and the dearer. Gear is an item like any other: it sits in your hold or in what you carry, stacks, and can be sold.

- **Where it comes from** - the **Outfitting** tab of every station (pick a quality at the top, then buy: ship gear is fitted at once if a slot is free, else it goes into your hold; automaton gear goes into your hold); **destroyed ships** sometimes drop it (bosses always, tougher ships better); on planets **pirates**, **big beasts** and **containers** (chests, lockers - vaults most often); and every **signal source** you complete rewards a piece (better the harder the signal, two from an insane one).
- **Ship gear** fits the ship's **internal** and **utility** slots (how many depends on its class): stat modules (shields, hull, thrusters, cargo racks), **weapon modifiers** (Focusing Lens: damage; Capacitor Bank: fire rate; Targeting Computer: range - for every weapon), **plating** (resistances) Fit it from the hold in the Automaton's inventory (click it, or drag it onto the Ship Gear row); right-click a fitted module to take it out. Weapons themselves go on the hardpoints (above).
- **The automaton's loadout** - its **equipment screen** shows the automaton with a slot at each part of it: the **weapon** in the right arm, a weapon mod in the right hand and one on the left arm, **armour** on the torso, the **core** in the head, the passives in the legs and on the back - 7 slots: a **weapon** (Laser Rifle, Pulse Carbine, Plasma Rifle, Rail Rifle, Cryo Rifle - each its own damage, rate, reach and damage type), two **weapon mods** (scope, amplifier, capacitor, stabiliser), **armour** (health and resistances), a **core** (healing, speed, longer overcharges) and two **passives**. Equip from the Automaton's inventory (gear in your hold) or the Field Computer's (gear you carry): click a piece, or drag it onto a slot; to take it off, **click the slot** (or drag it back onto your items, or right-click it) - it goes back where it came from, if there's room. Your stats change at once.
- **Damage types and resistances** - every hit is **energy** (pulse cannons, lasers, bolts, beams), **kinetic** (slugs, bites, rams), **explosive** (missiles), **heat** (plasma, fire breath, the volcanic beasts) or **cold** (frost). Resistance to a type takes that share off its hits (at most 75%). **Heat resistance** also eases Akrotiri's heat (your healing slows less), **cold resistance** the ice moons' footing (you're slowed less).

## shipyard | Shipyard | keywords: Buy the
Each station sells its empire's designs (and the independents'), a **tab per class** - interceptors, fighters, couriers, explorers, gunships, freighters, frigates, and the **capital ships**: cruisers, battleships and dreadnoughts - cheapest first, each with its hull, shields, speed, hold and hardpoints beside how they compare with your ship's. Within a class the dearer designs are the better ones; prices run from about 15,000 dr for an interceptor to millions for the great frigates - and far more for a capital ship. Every empire builds its own capital ships (for now drawn with its biggest hulls, larger), and a **war fleet** of six or more flies under one: a cruiser, a battleship from nine ships, a dreadnought leading a full twelve. Other ships carry weapons for their class too, firing from all over their hulls, and a salvaged wreck may give one of them up. Your current ship is traded in for 80% of what you paid for it (the fighter you start with counts as 2,500 dr, so it trades in for 2,000): you pay the difference. Cargo is kept; weapons go on the new ship's hardpoints that take them (the rest into your hold), and other fittings that don't fit it are sold back.


## designer | Designer | keywords: Skin, Apply paint, Factory paint
Repaint your ship with the hue, saturation, brightness and tint sliders, or pick a ready-made **skin** (a colour swatch with its price, ✓ when owned). **Apply paint** pays and paints; **Factory paint** restores the original colours for free.

## sell | Selling cargo | keywords: Sell all cargo
Sell your loot and trade goods at this station's prices, one at a time, all of one kind, or **all cargo** at once (missiles and story items are kept).

## empire | Empires, independents and your reputation | keywords: Reputation, Independent, Independents, outpost, forward base, Hostile, Unfriendly, Cordial, Friendly, Allied
You answer to no empire: what counts is your **reputation** with each of them - and with the **Independents** - from -100 to 100, in tiers: **Hostile** (below -50: their warships attack you, their stations refuse you, prices +15 %), **Unfriendly** (-50 to -15: prices +10 %), **Neutral**, **Cordial** (15: prices -2 %, Trusted missions), **Friendly** (40: -5 %, Honoured missions, bounties +10 %) and **Allied** (70: -10 %, Hero missions, bounties +25 %). The station's **Reputation** tab shows where you stand with everyone.

- **Raising it** (slowly - a mission adds 0.1 to 0.4): missions at their stations; trading there (every 10,000 dr bought or sold: +1); hunting Sea Peoples raiders in their space.
- **Losing it**: attacking their ships - the first shot at one costs 2, each one destroyed 8 (their war enemies think a little better of you); shooting down a civilian in another empire's space annoys that empire too. It takes several ships to turn an empire against you, and a bad name fades back toward Neutral by about 1 a minute.
- **Independents**: free ports and ships that answer to no empire. Neutral with everyone and at war with no one - only the Sea Peoples prey on them. A quarter of the civilian ships you meet are independent.
- **Combined invasions and distress calls**: an invasion gathers **two or three fleets** at a staging system on the border, each from a system of its own; when they're all there (or after two minutes) they set out together. A station under attack sends a **distress call**: the nearest idle defence fleets of its owner - and of the owner's **allies** at war with the attacker - within 4 jumps answer it (two at most); allies go home when the danger is over.
- **War missions** (from stations of empires at war, or with an invasion coming): **Protect** a system an invasion is heading for (destroy so many of the invader's warships there), **Strike** an enemy station (take a share of its condition off - it costs you standing with its owner), **Join** one of their fleets (fly within 1,600 of its ships for a minute or more, wherever it goes) or **Raid** an enemy fleet (destroy so many of its ships, wherever it goes).
- **Fleets and invasions**: every empire keeps **war fleets** of 3 to 12 warships. Defence fleets hold its systems (about one for every three) and hurry to a besieged system nearby; at war, an empire gathers **invasion fleets** against the enemy systems on its border (the news tells you). Where fleets of empires at war meet, they fight; an invasion with no defenders left **besieges** the stations of the empires it's at war with - and once the owner has no station left in a system, the system falls to the invader. In the system you're in, the fleets are real ships, and a fleet flies and fights **as one**: on patrol or on its way, its warships keep a **wedge** behind their leader; in a fight they all take **one target** (the leader's, or whichever foe one of them engaged) and spread out in an **arc** round it at their firing distance, the arc swinging round as the leader circles. **Attack one ship and the whole fleet counter-attacks**. You see the invaders go for the stations, and you can join either side (attacking an empire's ships still costs you standing with it). A peace sends invasions home.
- **Damaged stations**: a station worn down below 40 % **burns** - flames and smoke on it - and offers only crisis jobs: **Repairs** (bring materials: machinery, ore, energy cells, electronics - it mends the station, and raises your standing with its owner) and, while it's besieged, **Defend** (destroy so many of the besieger's warships in the system). Stations mend slowly once a siege is over. At 0 a station is **destroyed for good** (the home system's stations can burn but never fall).
- **Who runs the stations**: in every system the empire holding it runs most of the stations. The others are **independent** free ports, an ally's **outpost** (opened with the owner's leave, when they are on good terms and the ally holds a system next door) or a **forward base** of an empire at war with the owner - it wears the system's control down from inside, and with it the system may fall. When a system changes hands, the loser's stations there go to the winner; an outpost of an empire no longer welcome declares itself independent. The galaxy page and the sector map show a station's owner when it isn't the system's.

## sandbox | Making a living: the towns' people, couriers, pilots | keywords: ore buyer, courier, package, local pilot, ride, scanner, bounty voucher, first ship
Every city has three people by its **landing field**: click one to talk.
- **The ore buyer** pays for the raw ore in your pack - what your mining beam cuts from a world's deposits (fire at one; see [Mining on foot](doc:digging)).
- **The courier's office** gives you a **package** for a town on another world of the system or for one of its stations, and what it pays on delivery (about 300-480 dr). You carry it in both hands - no rifle, no running; **H** sets it down and picks it up again (or click it). Hand it over at the town's courier's office, or at the station's harbour office (its officer, or the Missions terminal).
- **The local pilot** flies you to a town on another world or to a station for a small fee: his ship comes down on the field, and he walks over to it, up its ramp and through it to the pilot's seat at its consoles. Walk up the ramp after him (the passenger seat beside his is yours); it takes off once you're in and he's seated, and he flies you there - and stays at the controls when you walk down the ramp.
- **The scanner** (**Z**, or the scanner in hand and the left button - on foot): its pulse marks for a minute the ore deposits and the [veins in the ground](doc:terrain) near you, and the places round you - towns, caves, dungeons, pirate camps, lairs, armed creatures - with their names and distances.
- **Your first ship**: a station's shipyard (in its port's services hall) sells them - the cheapest about 13,800 dr, a few dozen deliveries and the tutorial's rewards. Bought, it comes down that port's lift onto a pad. Until then, the local pilots and the traders (walk up a trader's ramp in a port - it takes you wherever it goes) are how you get about.
- **Bounties**: a pirate raider destroyed earns a **bounty voucher**, handed in at any station's harbour office (its officer, or the Missions terminal).

## tutorial | The tutorial | keywords: Tutorial, F2, steps, reward
A new game's tutorial is a small panel at the top right: the next thing to learn, and what it pays. It never stops you - do the steps in any order, or go your own way: each is paid when you do it. On foot: walking, the jet pack, the maps, the scanner, mining, selling ore, a courier's package (and setting it down), a ride with a local pilot, delivering it, your first ship. Then your ship: the controls, undocking, the Hyperion drive, docking, calling your ship, two raiders, their bounty vouchers. Got your ship another way? Once you've flown it, docked and fought, the tutorial ends and pays every reward it would have. It's kept in your saves; **F2** hides or shows it.

![A new game: on foot on Amnissos by a city's landing field - its ore buyer, courier's office and local pilot - the tutorial's panel top right, the scanner's marks.](shot:space3d_start)

- **Missions** (each station's Missions tab; eight on offer): up to five at once - Pirate Sweep, Hunt, Courier, Supply Run (deliver trade goods to another station), Salvage Request / Mining Contract (bring salvage or ore here), Survey (fly to an uncharted point, marked on your map). Four tiers - Routine, Trusted, Honoured, Hero - need reputation 0 / 10 / 25 / 50 with the station's empire and pay 1x / 1.5x / 2.2x / 3.2x; the ones you aren't trusted with yet are greyed out and can't be taken. Each finished mission raises your reputation with that empire (+1 / +2 / +3 / +4). **Turn in** salvage and mining jobs for the reward; **Abandon** frees a slot. **Pay** follows how hard a job is: its tier (Routine, Trusted, Honoured, Hero) and how dangerous its kind (a courier run or a survey is safe; supply, salvage and repairs a little risky; bounties, joining a fleet and defence dangerous; hunts, strikes, protecting a system and raiding fleets the most) - from about 500 dr for a Routine courier run to tens of thousands for a Hero-tier fight.

# computer-ch | The Automaton
The automaton's own computer (Tab): your inventory and toolbar, the maps and the Archive.

## computer | The Automaton | keywords: Close the Automaton, Inventory, Toolbar, Archive, Map, Planet, Solar system
Press **Tab** (or **I**) to open it - always on the **Inventory**; the game goes on while it's open, and it closes by itself if you're attacked. Tabs (keys **1-3**): **Inventory** (your inventory, your toolbar, the automaton's equipment), **Map** (its own three tabs: **Planet** - the [planet map](doc:planet-map), **Solar system** - the [solar map](doc:sector-map), **Galaxy** - the [galaxy map](doc:galaxy); **M** opens it on the planet's map on a planet, else the solar map, **G** on the galaxy) and the **Archive** (every book of the game). Refining and making things aren't here: they're your ship's own devices, each with its own window (see [The ship's devices](doc:industry)).

**Your inventory** - everything you own, in stacks of up to 100 a slot (your ship's cargo space sets how many slots: at least 12); drag stacks to arrange it, click gear to equip it on the automaton (or drag it onto the automaton's equipment screen beside it).

**The toolbar** - the automaton's nine slots (a new game starts with its tools on **1-5**: the pulse rifle, the mining beam, the terrain digger, the ground scanner and the builder - the rest you fill). Drag anything usable onto a slot (in the Inventory, or onto the toolbar at the bottom of the screen), or hover it and press **1-9**; drag a slot onto another to swap them, off the bar (or right-click it) to empty it. A slot shows the thing's icon and how many you have; pressing its key (or clicking it) uses it:
- **The automaton's tools** (the Inventory's **TOOLS** row): the **rifle** and the **mining beam** - the rifle out (the digger put away), the **terrain digger** - out in place of the rifle (again: the rifle back), the **ground scanner** - in hand, the **left button** sends its pulse (**Z** sends one whatever's in hand). The **builder** - in hand, a preview of a [building piece](doc:building) where you aim; the left button places it. The slot of what's in the automaton's hands is lit.
- **Gear, equipped or not** (from the automaton's equipment screen or your inventory): not yet on - equipped (a weapon brought out); on - lit, and a weapon brought out.
- **Supplies**: **food** and **energy drinks** give stamina back, **medicine** heals the automaton on foot.



## industry | The ship's devices: refinery, fabricator, upgrade kits | keywords: Industry, Refinery, Fabricator, Refine, Make, Upgrade Kit, Fit, Fragments, device
Your ship's own devices, each at its terminal aboard with its own window (walk up to it and click it): the **Refinery** in the cargo bay and the **Fabricator** on the bridge. Their work goes on in the background while you fly (a queue on the right - ✕ stops a job and gives back what wasn't used).

- **Refinery** (equipment, outfitters' SYSTEMS; the cargo bay): turns the **fragments** your mining laser cuts into their minerals, a unit each (1.2 s a unit; the reactor's refinery upgrade makes it faster) - worth two and a half times as much. Rubble gives scrap and now and then a mineral.
- **Fabricator** (equipment; the hull): makes things from minerals and goods - over thirty **recipes** in five groups: **materials** (bronze ingots, girders, hull plates, rivets, glass, power cables, coolant, fuel, water), **components** (bearings, circuit boards, capacitor banks, processors, servos, optic fibre, tools, reactor coils), **supplies** (missiles), small **weapons** (extra-small pulse and plasma cannons, a missile launcher) and **Upgrade Kits**. Each card shows what it takes (what you have of each), how long and what it sells for: the markets buy the materials and components - mining, refining and making things is a living.
- **Kits** (the Fabricator's second page) - fit a component upgrade yourself: a **Mk I** kit raises a stat from level 0 or 1, a **Mk II** from 2 or 3, a **Mk III** from 4 to the top (the same stats as a station's UPGRADES).


## planet-map | The planet map and town plans | keywords: Planet map, Planet, Town plan, Whole world, Find yourself, Known on this world, Globe, Back
The Automaton's **Map > Planet** (**M** on a planet): the world you're on - or the nearest, or one picked on the solar map (**Planet map** beside a world's details) - as a **3D globe** made from its real ground: its seas and shallows, shores, uplands and peaks, ice and lava, the relief raised so you can read it, a grid every 30°. **Drag** to turn it (slower the nearer you are), the **wheel** zooms in toward the cursor, a middle click (or **Home**, or **Whole world**) shows the whole world, **Find yourself** turns it to you; the keys and the pad turn and zoom it like the other maps.

**Fog of war**: only the ground **you've seen** shows - about 300 m round you on foot, wider the higher you fly (up to 2.6 km) - remembered planet by planet, in your saves; the rest is a dark haze with only its shape showing. Where you've seen them, the map marks the world's **towns** (a city's mark has its bar), **caves** and **dungeons**, and **pirate camps**; **you** (a white dot pointing your way) and **your ship** always. **Click** a mark for its details beside the globe - what it is, whose town, where (latitude, longitude) and how far from you; **Known on this world** lists everything you've found (click a line to turn to it). The title says how much of the world you've explored.

**Town plans**: a town **you've walked into** has its plan - zoom in over it and the globe keeps closing in on it while its plan fades in over the ground, laid where the town is, its names coming in as you near, until the plan is all there (click the town, or **Town plan**, for the same dive in one go): the town from above, north up: its palace and houses, the shrine and the storehouse, the paved square, the landing field - and its **points of interest** named: the **palace**, **shrine**, **storehouse**, **landing field** and, by a city's field, the **ore buyer**, the **courier's office** and the **local pilot** ([Making a living](doc:sandbox)); you and your ship on it, a scale and a north arrow. The wheel zooms it on, dragging pans it, a middle click fits it; zoom out past the whole town (or **Back**, **Home**) and it fades back into the globe. A town you've only seen from afar has no plan: the globe goes only so near.

![](shot:town_plan3d)


## sector-map | The solar map | keywords: Map, Solar map, Solar system, Set course, Clear course, Look at it, Whole system, Find your ship, Known in this system, Planet map
The map of the system you're in (the Automaton's **Map > Solar system**, **M**), in 3D: its star, the planets and moons on their orbits, the stations, the jump gates, asteroid fields, bio-signatures, the ships your sensors see - and you - over the system's plane, a polar grid of rings 10 km apart. **The worlds move**: each goes round its star (the further out, the slower), each moon round its world, every orbit drawn in its world's colour; a station or an asteroid field in a world's orbit goes round with it, and the map shows them all where they are now - as in space. The world you're on (or flying low over) is always shown, and any world you've once seen stays known wherever its orbit takes it. Each thing hangs over the plane on a thin stem, so you can tell how high above or below it it lies. **Drag** to turn the map, **right or middle drag** (or **Shift + drag**) to pan, the **wheel** zooms toward the cursor; a click of the middle button (or **Home**) shows the whole system, **Find your ship** flies the view back to you, a **double click** flies it to what's under the cursor. From the keyboard or a pad: **WASD**, the arrows, the D-pad or the left stick turn it, the right stick pans, **+ / -**, **Page Up / Down** or the triggers zoom.

**Click** anything for its details in the panel beside the map: a world's kind, size, orbit, moons, towns and whether you can land on it; a station's empire, economy, condition, your standing and whether you know its market; where a gate leads and whether you've been there (and if it's the next gate of your route); a ship's kind, flag, hull and speed; and how far it is from you and how high over the plane. **Set course** (or **Enter**, **Space**, pad **A**) makes it your target - the HUD points the way, a flowing orange line on the map runs to it, and the **Hyperion drive** (**J**) takes you there; **Clear course** drops it; **Planet map** (a world picked) shows it on the [planet map](doc:planet-map). **Backspace** (pad **X**) picks the next thing, nearest first; the list under the panel (**Known in this system**) names everything you know here - click a line to pick it.

**Fog of war**: only what your sensors have swept - about 28 km round your ship, wherever you've flown - shows; the rest of the plane is a dark haze, its worlds, stations, gates and fields hidden until you get near them. The orange ring on the plane is your sensors' reach. The star, you and your target always show; ships only while your sensors see them. What you've swept is remembered, system by system (a system **charted** from its navigation beacon shows all of it). **Trade** (the cart button, or **T**) shows the best trade runs from the stations you know here: green arrows to another station, or to the gate on the way to a station up to two jumps away (named on the tag), with the good to carry and the profit a unit.

![](shot:map3d)


## nav-reports | Navigation reports | keywords: nav beacon, report, sell, chart
Scan a system's **navigation beacon** (right-click it, then stay within 1.6k for 6 seconds) and it gives you a **navigation report** of the system as it is right now - it doesn't lift the fog (your sensors still have to find things on the map), it tells you what's there. The report opens at once: the system's **stations** (and who holds each), its **jump gates** (and where they lead), its **planets and moons** (the landable ones in green), the **ships** about - **hostile** ones by who they are (pirates, an empire at war with you), **friendly and neutral** ones by empire, and all of them by trade (traders, miners, patrols...) - any **monsters**, and how many asteroids, wrecks and signals there are. Right-click the beacon again while you're still in the system to see it again (✕ or Esc closes it).

A copy goes into your hold - **one a visit**: leave the system and come back for another. **Stations in other systems buy reports** (Sell tab): the further the report's system is from theirs, the more they pay - 60 drachmas, plus 70 for every jump between the two systems and 10 for each of its stations. In its own system a report is worthless. Hover a report in your hold for its summary.


## galaxy | The galaxy | keywords: Galaxy, Plot route, Clear route, Add waypoint, Whole galaxy, uncharted
**Galaxy space** - **New Hellas** - reached only through the jump gates: **120 star systems** spread through a 3D volume, linked by gate lanes. Each has an owner - the **Minoan Thalassocracy**, the **Athenian League**, the **Spartan Hegemony**, the **Mycenaean Kingdoms**, the **Ionian League**, the **Cycladic Isles** (each holding 16 to 18 systems round its heartland) - or the Sea Peoples (seventeen dens). The **Cycladic Isles** are the oldest seafarers of the Aegean: white marble and black obsidian ships and stations, folded-arm figurines, spirals and longboats; friends of the Minoans, wary of the mainland. Empires go to war and make peace; border systems change hands.

The **galaxy map** (the Automaton's **Map > Galaxy**, **G**) shows it in 3D, over the galactic plane: each system a star in its own colour, ringed in its owner's, a stem dropping from it to the plane; the empires' territories glow round their systems like clouds; lanes between systems run in their owners' colours, war fronts flow in red, an orange arc turns round a system in a crisis, and an orange ring pulses round the one you're in. It turns, pans and zooms like the solar map (drag, right drag, the wheel; keys and pad the same; **Whole galaxy** or **Home** shows all you know). **Fog of war**: only the systems **you've been in** show (Knossos from the start), with the lanes between them; a lane leading off to a system you haven't visited fades out toward a faint **?** - the gate's sign names it, nothing more is known until you go.

**Click** a system for its details beside the map: its owner, star, planets and moons, state, pirate activity, its stations (the ones you know by name), whether you've been there, your standing with its owner and whom they're at war with, and how far it is - in jumps along the lanes you know, and in light-years. **Plot route** (or **Enter**, **Space**, pad **A**) plans the shortest way there through the gates you know (an uncharted system next to them counts): an orange line flows along it on the map, your course is set to the first gate, and after each jump to the next - the HUD points you to each in turn; **Clear route** removes it. **Shift + click** a system (or **Add waypoint**) adds it to the end of the route - the route goes on from there, so you can go round several systems in one trip. Stray off the route and it's planned again from where you are. **Trade routes** (the cart button, or **T**) turns on the trade layer: the best runs between systems (buy at a station, sell at one up to two jumps away - one run a pair of systems, the ten best) as green arrows along the gate lanes, labelled with the good and the profit a unit, the best brightest; pick one good or all of them. The right column lists them; click one to plot a route to where you buy. They follow the prices as they move. Fly into a gate to jump. Each gate is a great armoured ring around a turning blue vortex, glowing faintly in the colour of the empire that owns the system it leads to; a ring of light bursts out of it as you go through, and again from the gate you come out of.

![](shot:galaxy3d)

- **Planets and moons**: every system beyond Knossos has 1 to 12 planets, each one of the four kinds you know from home - **volcanic** worlds (like Akrotiri) close to the star, **ocean** worlds (like Amnissos) further out, **ice** worlds (like Ida) and **gas giants** (like Dikte) at the edge. Some have **moons** - grey, cratered little worlds like Kamares, named after their planet (Gournia I, Gournia II...); gas giants can have up to three. You can land on every one of them: each has its kind's land, beasts and climate (the heat of a volcanic world, the ice underfoot), but its own map and name. The galaxy page counts a system's planets and moons; on the solar map a moon's name shows once you zoom in.

# planets-ch | Planets
Landing, walking, the animals, the towns and the pirates of the worlds.

## planets | On the surface | keywords: Land on, Take off
- **Landing** - low and slow over dry, level ground clear of trees and boulders, **L**: the ship sets down on its legs (the readout says why not, when it can't). **U** stands you up from the pilot's seat; walk back through the ship and down the ramp. Walk up the ramp and click the pilot's seat to take the controls; at the controls, **L** or **Space** takes off.
- **On foot** - **W A S D** walk where the camera looks, **Shift** runs, **Space** jumps - hold it and your **jet pack** fires, the mouse looks round. Shallows are waded, deep water swum - head above the water, a front crawl; **F / Ctrl** dives under (a breaststroke), **Space** brings you back up, and between the two you drift slowly up. The **left button** fires your rifle; the sights show what they're on. Out of health, your ship's drones bring you back beside it.
- **Under the sea** - the ocean worlds' seas have their own life: kelp forests and sea-grass meadows swaying in the current, corals, sponges, urchins and boulders on the floor (solid: swim round them), schools of fish that scatter as you come, rays, an eel or sea serpent, glowing jellyfish. The light falls through the water in shafts and ripples over the floor; the deeper, the darker and bluer; look up and the surface shines over you.

![](shot:space3d_underwater)
- **Plants** - each world grows its own: trees, conifers, bushes, grass, flowers, crystals, fungi, cacti - from its seed and type, swaying in the wind.
- **Animals** - the forest worlds teem with the Greek animals and their strange cousins: Cretan wild goats, sheep, red deer, donkeys, hares, foxes, tortoises, little owls, golden eagles, wolves, wild boars, snakes, striped tigrokeros, mushroom mammoths, glowing selas stags, capped slugs, bubble toads, moss pangolins, aeromantas, sky jellies, harpyx raptors, hoplorhinos, giant mantises, drakaina serpents, beetles and bugs, moths, fireflies, dragonflies, spiders and centipedes - a handful of kinds a world, always a hunter among them. The ice worlds have ice stags, shard crawlers, ice hares, frost rays, ice wisps, frost wolves, frost beasts and ice wyrms; the volcanic worlds magma behemoths, cinder stalkers, obsidian mantises, lava serpents, pyrohounds, ash wraiths, basalt golems and fumarole titans. Grazers run from you, skittish ones bolt sooner, birds take off, **predators** hunt you and bite.
- **The jet pack** - on your automaton's back. Jump, keep **Space** held, and it fires: you climb while its charge lasts (a bar under your sights), and it fills again on the ground. Upgrade it (a station's Workshop - **Upgrades**, the automaton's **Leg Servos**: **Jet pack**, five levels) and it burns longer and harder; at the fifth it never runs out - climb out of the air into **space**, hover when you let go, **F / Ctrl** to come down, **W A S D** faster the higher you are (**Shift**: faster still) - and fly to another world and land on it, no ship needed. Flying free high up or out in space, **B** calls your ship: it comes to you and you're aboard (a marker shows where it is whenever you're off the ground). Land gently: a fall of more than a few storeys hurts - hold the jet on the way down to brake.
- **Towns** - the inhabited worlds (ocean and ice worlds of the empires) have their towns: a **city** round its **palace** - wings of one to three storeys round a central court, a colonnade of red columns (wider at the top, dark capitals), fresco bands, horns of consecration on the roofs, a gateway, an altar, a grand staircase up onto the roofs - and **villages** of flat-roofed houses on their lanes, a shrine, a storehouse with its jars. Each empire builds its own way: **Minoan** ochre plaster and timber, red columns, horns, running spirals; **Athenian** marble blocks, white Doric columns, the meander, a colonnaded temple under a tiled gable; **Spartan** grey limestone on a crimson foot, bronze shields on the walls, lambdas; **Mycenaean** walls of great many-sided blocks, a gold band, a beehive tholos for a shrine; **Ionian** marble between lapis bands, slim lapis columns under gold volutes, gold armillaries on the roofs; **Cycladic** whitewashed cubes with blue bands and blue domes, marble figures before the chapel. Its **people** walk its streets, each empire its own: the Minoans' **palace guards** (terracotta ceramic, a painted fan crest, laser rifles) and **androids** in a triceratops's image - a great painted frill, long brow horns, a red cape - armed with a **laser rifle**, a **laser bow** or a **labrys**, the Minoan double axe; Athens' horned, owl-eyed machines in marble and navy; Sparta's crested tyrants in iron and crimson; Mycenae's gold-domed masks; Ionia's lapis duck-bills with their long gold crests; the Cyclades' pale idols. They turn to look at you - and take on the pirates and hunting beasts that come near. By every city's landing field stand its **ore buyer**, **courier's office** and **local pilot** (see [Making a living](doc:sandbox)). Every town has a **landing field** beside it; from orbit the towns of the planet you're near are on your screen - **T** targets one, the Hyperion drive takes you there. Climb the stairs and walk the roofs. **Walk in**: every building has its doorway - the palace's wings open onto the court, their rooms one through another (the **throne room** in the west wing), stairs up to the upper floors; the houses have their hearths, benches, jars and beds upstairs. Indoors a warm light goes with you.

![](shot:space3d_inside)
- **Pirate camps** - a tent, crates and a mast with a red light: their guards, pirate androids, open fire when you come near.
- **Caves and dungeons** - every rocky world hides two **caves** (a dark mouth in an arch of boulders) and two **dungeons** (a stone gateway with horns of consecration) - a click at one goes down. Below: rooms and passages lit by torches - a cave's rough rock, stalactites and stalagmites; an old labyrinth's dressed stone and red pillars - and the stairs back up where you came in. Their dead walk: **skeleton warriors** with bronze helmets, round shields and short swords come for you in the rooms; deeper in, **demons** hurl fire from afar and claw up close; in the deepest room a **demon lord** guards a **chest** (click it to open it: drachmas). The walls stop your bolts and theirs. Downed below, your ship's drones carry you out.

![](shot:space3d_dungeon)

![](shot:space3d_cave)
- **Leaving** - board, and **L** or **Space**.
